evaluated various validation data sources for operational use, each with its own strengths and weaknesses, including high water marks (HWMs) (Breaker et al., [2016](#page-27-27); Musser et al., [2017;](#page-29-32) Watson et al., [2017\\)](#page-30-30), remote sensing observations (Aristizabal et al., [2020;](#page-27-9) Aristizabal & Judge, [2021\\)](#page-27-10), and modeled extents from hyper-resolution, local models (McEnery et al., [2005](#page-29-4)).","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0002","evidenceText":"This data set was selected due to its large spatial coverage, availability of cross-sections with streamflow information, higher level of sophistication when compared to HAND, engineering scale detail, and a storied use in the literature as an evaluation data set (Afshari et al., [2018](#page-27-11); Bates et al., [2016;](#page-27-28) Cook & Merwade, [2009;](#page-27-29) Criss & Nelson, [2022;](#page-27-30) Follum et al., [2017](#page-28-30); Hu & Demir, [2021](#page-28-31); Li & Demir, [2022](#page-28-32); Li et al., [2022;](#page-28-33) Rajib et al., [2016;](#page-29-33) Wing et al., [2017;](#page-30-31) Wing et al., [2017](#page-30-31); Zheng, Maidment, et al., [2018](#page-30-12); Zheng, Maidment, et al., [2018](#page-30-12)).","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0003","evidenceText":"We selected 49 available HUC8s, shown in Figure [7](#page-16-0), which span about 185 thousand km2 across nine states.","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0004","evidenceText":"The maps of the 1% recurrence flow (1 in 100 years) and the 0.2% recurrence flow (1 in 500 years) are furnished by InFRM as well as the corresponding discharges and mapping extents for evaluation.","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0005","evidenceText":"We did exclude NWM V2.1 Reservoirs from evaluation because these are not properly accounted for in the inundation sourced from OWP FIM.","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0006","evidenceText":"By using the same HEC-RAS derived discharges and FIM extents for creating maps with OWP FIM, we are able to separate out errors introduced by NWM inputs and processes including land surface interactions, groundwater fluxes, atmospheric forcings, hydraulic routing, and others that would have potentially affected our conclusions if we had used NWM forecasted discharges.","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0007","evidenceText":"Figure [8](#page-16-1) illustrates both NWM V2.1 and BLE flowpaths as well as the BLE cross-sections that have recurrence discharges associated with them.","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0008","evidenceText":"We elected to spatially intersect the HEC-RAS cross sections with the NWM stream network assigning the 1% and 0.2% flow rates to each NWM reach.","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0009","evidenceText":"Additionally, the stream network of the InFRM furnished models are of higher stream densities and bifurcation ratios, as evident in Figure [8](#page-16-1), leading to a significant amount of FNs along headwater streams with unit Horton-Strahler order due to the lack of representation of these additional headwater streams in the NWM network.","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0010","evidenceText":"The metrics employed in this study to evaluate inundation extents include CSI, Probability of Detection (POD), and False Alarm Ratio (FAR) and are presented in Equations [6](#page-17-0)[–8,](#page-17-1) respectively.","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0011","evidenceText":"To calculate these secondary metrics, one must define three primary metrics starting with true positives (TP) which is predicted wet and wet in the BLE benchmark data set. The two types of errors consist of false positives (FP), or type I errors, which is dry in the benchmark but predicted wet and false negatives (FN), or type II errors, which is wet in the benchmark but predicted dry.","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0012","evidenceText":"Lastly, the reader may come across true negatives (TN) which is defined as dry in both","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0013","evidenceText":"Maximizing POD indicates a model's ability to detect the given threat of interest, inundation, while minimizing FAR is sought to indicate a models ability in reducing FN errors.","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0014","evidenceText":"In other words, POD is an indicator of model skill in inundated regions while FAR is an indicator of model skill in non-inundated regions.","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0015","evidenceText":"This creates additional inundation areas in the validation data that are not modeled with our HAND based FIMs.","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0016","evidenceText":"While these metrics are commonly employed in the evaluation of FIM and binary weather prediction communities in general, they do come with some notable limitations including frequency dependence in the case of CSI and FAR (Gerapetritis & Pelissier, [2004](#page-28-34); Jolliffe & Stephenson, [2012](#page-28-35); Schaefer, [1990;](#page-29-34) Stephens et al., [2014](#page-30-32)).","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0017","evidenceText":"Lastly, approximately six HUC8s do not have NWM MS reaches thus we imputed the metrics for FR for these sites as the best available forecasting capability to compare GMS metrics to","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0018","evidenceText":"On the other hand, relying on point sources of streamflow or stage, such as gages, would eliminate this limitation, but limit the information available to only a single source of inundation at a specific site.","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0019","evidenceText":"Our HAND based approach coupled with SRCs requires streamflow as input and is agnostic as to the source of that streamflow whether forecasted, observed, or probablistic. Due to this fact, evaluation of our relative elevation CFIM method was conducted by comparison to the HEC-RAS 1D models produced within FEMA region 6 (Base Level Engineering (BLE) Tools and Resources, [2021](#page-27-21); estBFE Viewer, [2021;](#page-30-22) USACE, [2022\\)](#page-30-23).","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0020","evidenceText":"evaluation of our relative elevation CFIM method was conducted by comparison to the HEC-RAS 1D models produced within FEMA region 6","locatorAnchor":null},{"evidenceSpanID":"evidence-0021","evidenceText":"the stream network of the InFRM furnished models are of higher stream densities and bifurcation ratios","locatorAnchor":null}]}
